title: Daily Health Briefing
intro: Good morning! Today's digest pulls recent, reputable findings across your tracked topics — anti-aging, HIIT for women, pelvic floor training, integrative options for HER2+/TP53 breast cancer, and sleep. Sources are drawn from PubMed, JAMA Network, NIH/NCBI, Nature, Frontiers, and specialty societies; citations render as chips beneath each section. Informational only — talk with a clinician before acting on anything here.

sections.body:
This week the standout is **urolithin A (UA)** moving beyond muscle into **immune aging**, plus a useful reality-check comparing the big three "longevity" supplements.

- **UA and the aging immune system.** A 2025 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in *Nature Aging* (50 healthy middle-aged adults, **1,000 mg/day for 4 weeks**) found UA expanded **naive-like, less-exhausted CD8+ T cells**, boosted their fat-oxidation capacity, and increased mitochondrial biogenesis — early evidence that a mitophagy activator can nudge "inflammaging" in the right direction (NCT05735886).
- **Not all longevity supplements are equal.** A comparative narrative review (evidence through **April 2026**) concluded that, of urolithin A, spermidine, and NAD+ precursors (NR/NMN), **UA has the most coherent human evidence** — aligned mechanism, biomarker, and early functional data for mitochondrial health, muscle endurance, and immune aging. **Spermidine** remains biologically plausible but clinically unvalidated, and **NR/NMN reliably raise NAD+ biomarkers** but still lack proof of broad anti-aging benefit.
- **Context on effect size.** Even UA's best trials show **modest, biomarker-level** effects (e.g., the JAMA Network Open muscle-endurance RCT was safe and improved endurance/biomarkers, but missed its 6-minute-walk primary endpoint).

Practical framing: favor supplements with actual human RCTs, expect **small** effects, and treat single-molecule "reverse aging" claims with skepticism.

sections.body:
New 2026 data reinforce HIIT as a **time-efficient** way to improve the heart and fitness in women — while meta-analyses keep it honest about where it does and doesn't beat steady-state cardio.

- **Better heart efficiency (RCT).** In an *International Journal of Obesity* (2026) trial, 25 women with obesity did **8 weeks of HIIT (4×4 min at 85–95% of max HR)** or moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT). Both improved myocardial deformation, but **only HIIT improved myocardial efficiency** — less "wasted work" and higher work efficiency — suggesting an edge for reversing subclinical cardiac dysfunction.
- **Fitness gains are real, but not magic.** A women-specific systematic review & meta-analysis found HIIT clearly raises **VO2max vs. no-exercise controls** (≈ +3–4 mL/kg/min), yet showed **no consistent superiority of HIIT over MICT** for VO2max — pick the format you'll actually stick with.
- **Reproductive-age women.** A separate meta-analysis found MICT slightly better for raw cardiorespiratory fitness, with **similar body-composition and metabolic results** — so HIIT earns its place mainly as a **time-saver**.

Bottom line: intensity buys cardio and metabolic benefit efficiently; **add resistance training**, progress gradually, and prioritize consistency over any single modality.

sections.body:
**Pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT)** stays the evidence-based **first-line** treatment for stress urinary incontinence (SUI). Fresh 2026 trials focus on *how* to train and *when* it can change the plan.

- **Training can postpone surgery.** A 2026 RCT in the *International Journal of Urogynecology* (90 women awaiting mid-urethral sling surgery) tested a **6-week intensive preoperative PFMT** program vs. education alone. The training group had large gains in muscle strength (Modified Oxford, *d* = 0.85) and symptom severity (*d* = 0.90), and — strikingly — **43% postponed their planned surgery**. Structured PFMT belongs in the pre-op pathway.
- **Biofeedback: helpful, but selectively.** A 2026 *Frontiers in Medicine* meta-analysis (8 RCTs, n = 1,045) found **EMG biofeedback added to PFMT** gives only a **small** extra reduction in incontinence severity (SMD −0.17) and mild quality-of-life benefit, but a **moderate** boost to muscle strength (SMD 0.56). Best reserved for women who struggle to identify the correct contraction.
- **Electrical stimulation.** A 2026 *Scientific Reports* RCT found adding **interferential current** to PFMT specifically reduced **weekly incontinence episodes**, without improving most other measures.

Key point: **correct technique and consistency beat sheer reps.** Confirm activation with a clinician or biofeedback; supervised programs generally outperform unsupervised ones.

sources.title: Effectiveness of Intensive Preoperative Pelvic Floor Muscle Training in Women with SUI Awaiting Surgery: A Randomized Controlled Trial

sections.topic: Alternative & Integrative Options — HER2+ / TP53 Breast Cancer
sections.body:
"Alternative" is best read as **evidence-based, integrative care alongside standard therapy** — never a replacement for HER2-targeted treatment. This week's theme is how **TP53/p53 status shapes drug choice**.

- **TP53 is common — and now actionable context.** In a 2026 *npj Breast Cancer* analysis of HER2+ tumors, **TP53 was mutated in ~47%** and **PIK3CA in ~24%**; PIK3CA mutations predicted **lower response (pCR)** to dual HER2 blockade. Mutation profiling is becoming part of planning, not an afterthought.
- **T-DXd works regardless of TP53.** An exploratory biomarker analysis of the **DESTINY-Breast03** trial (T-DXd vs. T-DM1) reported that **trastuzumab deruxtecan kept its superiority no matter the TP53, PIK3CA, HRR, or BRCA1/2 status** — reassuring for patients with p53-altered disease.
- **Why the payload matters.** Preclinical NIH/PMC work shows **HER2;p53 co-mutant** tumors are especially vulnerable to T-DXd's **TOP1-inhibitor payload**, and that **neratinib + T-DXd** is synergistic — now in a phase I trial (NCT05372614).
- **Integrative add-ons.** Correcting deficiencies (e.g., vitamin D) and coordinating any supplements with oncology remains the safe posture — some "natural" products can **interact with targeted therapy**, so clear them with your team first.

Framing: use integrative options as **clinician-approved add-ons**, and let mutation status inform — not replace — standard HER2-directed care.

sections.body:
For restless or disjointed sleep, 2026 guidance keeps **behavioral therapy ahead of pills and supplements** — with newer medications reserved as add-ons.

- **CBT-I stays first-line.** The AASM's 2026 guideline on *combination* therapy gave two conditional calls: CBT-I **plus** medication beats **medication alone**, but combination is **not** better than **CBT-I alone** — because CBT-I tends to deliver durable improvement without drug risks.
- **If a medication is needed, favor DORAs.** European (ESRS) guidance positions **dual orexin receptor antagonists** (e.g., daridorexant) for up to ~3 months, while older **hypnotics (benzodiazepines, Z-drugs) are short-term only (≤4 weeks)**. A 40-week extension study of **daridorexant** found it **safe and effective for up to a year with no tolerance or dependence** — useful for maintenance-type, disjointed sleep.
- **Supplements, honestly.** Guidelines note **melatonin is generally not effective for chronic insomnia disorder**; it helps most with **circadian problems** (jet lag, shift work) and mild sleep-onset trouble, especially in older adults.

Best-practice habits for restless/disjointed sleep:

1. Keep a **fixed wake time**, even on weekends.
2. Use the bed **for sleep only**; get up if awake ~15–20 minutes, and keep the room cool, dark, and quiet.
3. Dim lights and cut screens during a wind-down window; limit late caffeine and alcohol.
4. If fragmented sleep persists beyond a few weeks, see a provider to rule out **sleep apnea** and consider **CBT-I** (in-person or digital).
